title: What are the roles of the HTTP methods in RESTful APIs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS)?
shortTitle: What are the roles of the HTTP methods in RESTful APIs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS)

s1_definition.oneliner: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes, HEAD checks headers, and OPTIONS reports which methods are allowed.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **GET** – retrieves a representation of a resource, is safe (never changes state) and idempotent, and its responses are cacheable.
- **POST** – creates a new resource under a collection or triggers a process, is neither safe nor idempotent, and returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header.
- **PUT** – fully replaces a resource at a known URL, is idempotent, and missing fields are cleared because the body represents the whole resource.
- **PATCH** – partially updates a resource by sending only the changed fields, and is not guaranteed idempotent.
- **DELETE** – removes a resource and is idempotent, typically returning `204 No Content`.
- **HEAD** – returns only the status and headers of a GET response with no body, used to check existence or size.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's records room. GET is asking to see Rajesh's file without changing anything. POST is opening a new transfer slip, creating a fresh record. PUT is replacing Priya's entire profile form with a new one. PATCH is changing only Priya's phone number and leaving the rest. DELETE is shredding a beneficiary record. HEAD is asking whether Rajesh's file exists and how big it is, without pulling the whole file. OPTIONS is asking which actions are allowed on this file.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In a RESTful API every HTTP method has a defined role and defined properties around safety and idempotency. GET reads a resource and is both safe and idempotent, meaning it never changes server state and can be called repeatedly with the same result, which also makes it cacheable. POST creates a new resource under a collection and is neither safe nor idempotent, so two identical POSTs normally create two resources, which is why the server returns `201 Created` with a `Location` header.

PUT and PATCH are both updates but they mean different things. PUT is a full replacement and is idempotent, so if a client omits a field, PUT semantics say that field is cleared, because PUT means the body is the entire resource now. PATCH is a partial update where the client sends only the fields to change. In the beneficiary work at National Bank of India, when Priya wanted to change only the nickname of her landlord beneficiary, PATCH was the right verb, because sending a PUT with a missing account number would have wiped out that field.

DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent, returning `204 No Content`. HEAD returns only headers with no body, used to check existence cheaply. OPTIONS reports which methods a resource supports through the `Allow` header and handles CORS preflight.

The reason these properties matter beyond theory is retry behaviour. A proxy or client may safely retry a GET, PUT, or DELETE after a network timeout because repeating them is harmless. But it must never blindly retry a POST, because that could create a duplicate transfer and move Rajesh's money twice. So choosing the correct verb is not cosmetic: it directly protects correctness when the network is unreliable, which in a banking system is exactly where correctness matters most.

Remember one sentence: each HTTP method carries a contract about safety, idempotency, and cacheability that the entire ecosystem of clients, proxies, and caches depends on.

---

keyPoints: GET reads a resource and is safe and idempotent, meaning it never changes state and can be cached.
POST creates a new resource and is neither safe nor idempotent, returning 201 Created with a Location header.
PUT fully replaces a resource and is idempotent, so missing fields are cleared to defaults.
PATCH partially updates a resource by sending only changed fields and is not guaranteed idempotent.
DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent, typically returning 204 No Content.
HEAD returns only status and headers without a body, and OPTIONS reports allowed methods and handles CORS preflight.
The safety and idempotency contracts determine whether proxies and clients can safely retry a request after a network failure.
